items.title: Impact of postoperative hydrocortisone replacement dose on health-related quality of life and metabolic parameters in patients with cured Cushing's syndrome
items.summary: Single-center RCT (n=42) randomized post-op hypocortisolemic patients after curative Cushing's surgery to 15 mg/day vs. 30 mg/day hydrocortisone for 3 months. No quality-of-life difference between doses, but the 15 mg/day group had better triglycerides, total cholesterol, and HbA1c, with no excess adrenal crises. HPA axis recovery (71% overall) was independent of dose.
items.caveat: n=42, single-center, open-label -- quality of life is self-reported and unblinding could bias that specific outcome. Still directly actionable for a common bedside dosing decision.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old woman is 2 weeks post-transsphenoidal surgery for Cushing's disease, biochemically cured, now hypocortisolemic as expected. She asks whether she should take 'more' hydrocortisone to feel better faster. What do you tell her, and what do you monitor either way?
items.quiz_answer: Physiologic replacement (~15 mg/day range) is reasonable and was not worse for quality of life, while giving a better metabolic profile than 30 mg/day. There's no signal that 'more' speeds symptomatic recovery. Regardless of dose: monitor for adrenal insufficiency symptoms (fatigue, nausea, hypotension, hyponatremia), watch for cortisol withdrawal syndrome (myalgia, mood symptoms despite adequate replacement, which can mimic under-replacement), and track HPA axis recovery over time.

items.title: Is Hypercortisolism Treatable? Which Patients Should Be Treated and How-A Practical Guide for Clinicians.
items.summary: Narrative review synthesizing the CATALYST and MOMENTUM studies: confirmed hypercortisolism is rare in unselected T2D/hypertension populations (0.6-3.4%) but reaches roughly 1 in 4 in high-risk subgroups (treatment-resistant T2D, resistant hypertension, adrenal incidentalomas). The review argues against universal screening, recommending the overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test only for multiple/progressive/atypical cardiometabolic features or an incidentaloma.
items.caveat: This is a review restating CATALYST/MOMENTUM data, not new primary evidence -- useful for calibrating your own testing threshold, not a new finding in itself.
items.quiz_question: A patient with well-controlled T2D on one oral agent, normal BMI, and no cardiovascular risk factors or incidentaloma asks about cortisol testing. Per this review's logic, do they meet criteria for hypercortisolism screening?
items.quiz_answer: No -- this patient has none of the flagged features (treatment-resistant T2D, resistant hypertension, adrenal incidentaloma, or multiple/progressive/atypical cardiometabolic findings). The review argues against routine screening in exactly this kind of unselected, well-controlled presentation.

items.title: Hypertension action bundle including training of healthcare professionals to improve the detection of primary aldosteronism
items.summary: French hypertension clinic cohort (2016-2024): primary aldosteronism detection rose from 1.2 to 4.3 per 1,000 consultations alongside staff training on secondary hypertension screening. The reason for screening shifted over time, from classic hypokalemia/target-organ damage toward pre-eclampsia, refractory hypertension, and hypertension in young patients.
items.caveat: Single-center, observational -- shows association with a training intervention, not a validated new screening protocol. Useful signal for your own index of suspicion, not a guideline change.
items.quiz_question: Name two of the three 'newer' indications this cohort saw driving primary aldosteronism pickups in the later period, beyond classic hypokalemia.
items.quiz_answer: Pre-eclampsia, refractory hypertension, and hypertension in young patients.

items.title: Efficacy and safety of relacorilant for the treatment of patients with Cushing's syndrome (GRACE): a multicentre, phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised-withdrawal study.
items.summary: The GRACE trial randomized adults with endogenous hypercortisolism (Cushing's syndrome with hypertension and/or hyperglycemia) who had responded to open-label relacorilant to continue the drug or switch to placebo for 12 weeks. Significantly more placebo-assigned patients lost hypertension control compared to those maintained on relacorilant (proportion difference 34%; OR 0.17, p=0.022). Notably, no cases of adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy-associated vaginal bleeding, hypokalemia, or QT prolongation were observed, distinguishing relacorilant's safety profile from mifepristone.
items.caveat: Small randomized-withdrawal cohort (n=62 randomized); the open-label phase excluded non-responders, enriching for drug-sensitive patients and potentially overstating real-world efficacy. Study was industry-funded by Corcept Therapeutics, and primary endpoint was limited to hypertension response rather than broader remission criteria.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with Cushing's syndrome (ectopic ACTH excluded, not a surgical candidate) achieves good blood pressure control on relacorilant during an open-label phase. Based on the GRACE trial, what is the most likely consequence of switching her to placebo at that point, and what safety concern does NOT appear to be associated with relacorilant compared to mifepristone?
items.quiz_answer: Per GRACE, she has a significantly higher risk of losing hypertension control on placebo (proportion difference 34%, p=0.022). Unlike mifepristone, relacorilant was not associated with adrenal insufficiency, endometrial hypertrophy-related vaginal bleeding, hypokalemia, or QT prolongation in this trial.

items.title: Consensus Guidelines on Inferior Petrosal Sinus Sampling: A Guideline From the Society of Vascular and Interventional Neurology Guidelines and Practice Standards Committee.
items.summary: This multidisciplinary consensus guideline standardizes the full BIPSS workflow for distinguishing Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when biochemistry confirms ACTH-dependence but MRI is equivocal or shows a lesion under 6 mm. Key specifications include bilateral IPS catheterization with heparinization, CRH or desmopressin stimulation, a defined sampling protocol (2 pre-stimulation draws plus collections at 3, 5, 10, and 15 minutes post-stimulation), prechilled EDTA tubes with rapid ACTH processing, and prolactin measurement as an internal control. Interpretation cutoffs are IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio ≥2 pre-stimulation and ≥3 post-stimulation, with explicit guidance on recognizing false negatives.
items.caveat: Recommendations are graded by evidence level using a modified Delphi process; for many technical specifics the underlying RCT evidence is limited or absent, and much guidance is expert consensus. Institutional volume thresholds for competency are proposed but not yet validated against outcomes data.
items.quiz_question: You are evaluating a patient with biochemically confirmed ACTH-dependent Cushing's syndrome whose pituitary MRI shows a 4 mm equivocal lesion. You proceed to BIPSS. What stimulation agent is acceptable per the new SVIN guideline, what is the post-stimulation IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio cutoff for confirming pituitary origin, and why should prolactin be measured simultaneously?
items.quiz_answer: Either CRH or desmopressin is acceptable for stimulation. A post-stimulation IPS:peripheral ACTH ratio ≥3 confirms pituitary origin. Simultaneous prolactin measurement serves as an internal control to confirm that the IPS catheter is actually sampling venous effluent from the pituitary (adequate venous drainage), helping to identify potential false negatives due to inadequate catheter positioning.

items.title: Plasma ACTH Precursors measured by Pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) ELISA as a Predictor of Silent Corticotroph Adenomas.
items.summary: In a prospective observational cohort of 264 clinically non-functioning pituitary adenomas (CNFPAs), plasma POMC measured by a 2-site ELISA (detecting POMC and pro-ACTH but not mature ACTH) was markedly higher in silent corticotroph adenomas (SCAs) than in non-SCA tumors (median 73 vs. 14 fmol/mL, p<0.001). Elevated POMC (≥39 fmol/mL) identified SCA with 85.7% sensitivity and 97.9% specificity among CNFPAs. All known SCAs with visible residual tumor had elevated POMC, suggesting potential utility for post-surgical monitoring.
items.caveat: Surgically confirmed SCA subgroup was small (n=7 in the primary analysis), limiting the precision of sensitivity/specificity estimates. The POMC ELISA used is not commercially available in most centers. External validation in independent cohorts is required before clinical adoption.
items.quiz_question: A 55-year-old man has a 2 cm clinically non-functioning pituitary adenoma. Preoperative plasma POMC level returns at 95 fmol/mL (normal <39 fmol/mL). Based on this study, what does this finding suggest about the likely tumor subtype, and what pathophysiological mechanism underlies the elevated POMC?
items.quiz_answer: An elevated plasma POMC strongly suggests the tumor is a silent corticotroph adenoma (SCA). The underlying mechanism is defective post-translational processing of POMC — the tumor produces POMC and pro-ACTH but fails to cleave them into biologically active ACTH, explaining why these patients lack overt hypercortisolism despite harboring a corticotroph-lineage tumor.
items.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Mild autonomous ACTH secretion: a narrative review of 52 cases from the literature.
items.summary: This systematic literature review characterizes mild autonomous ACTH secretion (MAAS) — pituitary-derived hypercortisolism without overt Cushing's stigmata — across 52 published cases spanning 1994–2026. The condition affects a wide age range with female predominance (~60%), is found in roughly 5% of pituitary adenoma patients, and carries a high burden of metabolic comorbidity: hypertension in 56% and type 2 diabetes in 57%. A 1-mg DST cortisol >1.8 µg/dL with non-suppressed ACTH supports the diagnosis, while 24-hour urinary free cortisol and low-dose DST have limited sensitivity; surgical intervention often improves glycemic control and blood pressure, but lesions can be radiologically occult.
items.caveat: Retrospective case compilation (n=52 over 32 years) with substantial heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria, era, and reporting; the concept remains underdiagnosed and prospective data are lacking. Selection bias toward published/unusual cases is likely.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with resistant hypertension and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes is referred for evaluation. She has no Cushingoid features. Her 1-mg overnight DST cortisol is 2.4 µg/dL and her ACTH is 18 pg/mL (not suppressed). Her 24-hour urinary free cortisol is normal. What diagnosis should be considered, and what is the significance of the non-suppressed ACTH in this context?
items.quiz_answer: This biochemical pattern — post-DST cortisol >1.8 µg/dL with a non-suppressed ACTH — is consistent with mild autonomous ACTH secretion (MAAS), a pituitary-driven form of subclinical hypercortisolism. The non-suppressed ACTH distinguishes this from primary adrenal (ACTH-independent) mild autonomous cortisol secretion. Per this review, 24-hour UFC has limited sensitivity and a normal result does not exclude MAAS. Metabolic comorbidities such as her resistant hypertension and diabetes may reflect chronic cortisol excess, and surgical treatment has been associated with improvement in these parameters.
items.journal: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists

items.title: Endoscopic endonasal approach for adrenocorticotropic hormone-producing pituitary neuroendocrine tumor causing Cushing's disease: multicenter retrospective study on 162 patients with early postoperative cortisol assessment.
items.summary: This multicenter retrospective study of 162 patients with Cushing's disease undergoing endoscopic endonasal surgery found that morning cortisol <5 µg/dL in the first 3 postoperative days was a strong predictor of long-term remission (OR 0.25 for recurrence, p=0.003). A stricter threshold of <2 µg/dL on postoperative day 1 was associated with an even lower recurrence risk and a 91.8% recurrence-free survival at mean 29.8-month follow-up, though the difference between the two cutoffs was not statistically significant. These data support early postoperative hypocortisolemia as a robust remission biomarker and help refine the commonly used cortisol thresholds.
items.caveat: Retrospective multicenter design with heterogeneous institutional protocols and a relatively short mean follow-up (~30 months). The lack of statistical significance in direct comparison between <2 and <5 µg/dL thresholds limits firm conclusions about which cutoff is superior.
items.quiz_question: Following transsphenoidal resection for confirmed Cushing's disease, a patient's morning cortisol on postoperative day 2 is 3.8 µg/dL. How should this be interpreted, and what does this level predict for long-term remission based on this multicenter study?
items.quiz_answer: A cortisol of 3.8 µg/dL falls below the <5 µg/dL threshold, which in this study was independently associated with a significantly lower odds of recurrence (OR 0.25, p=0.003). While this patient does not achieve the stricter <2 µg/dL threshold (associated with 91.8% recurrence-free survival), the <5 µg/dL level within the first 3 postoperative days still constitutes a favorable prognostic sign for long-term remission and supports continued monitoring rather than early escalation of therapy.

items.title: Frequent antecedent nodules and diagnostic gaps in adrenocortical carcinoma.
items.summary: In a retrospective single-center series of 108 ACC patients with median follow-up of 86.7 months, 31.7% were found to have had antecedent adrenal nodules that appeared indolent for a median of 4.68 years before ACC diagnosis — directly challenging the prevailing dogma that ACC arises de novo without a measurable precursor lesion. Patients with antecedent nodules had a significantly higher risk of death (adjusted HR 2.9, 95% CI 1.39–6.0). Additionally, 31.4% underwent adrenal biopsy preoperatively, which was associated with increased risk of disease progression (adjusted HR 2.53) and death (adjusted HR 2.22), while mitotane therapy and locoregional treatments were associated with improved survival.
items.caveat: Single-center tertiary referral series (n=108) spanning 25 years, subject to referral bias and evolving imaging/diagnostic practices. Antecedent nodule identification relied on retrospective chart review, and causality between prior nodule and subsequent ACC cannot be established with certainty.
items.quiz_question: A 54-year-old patient has a 2.5 cm adrenal nodule on CT that has been stable in size for 3 years with an attenuation of 18 HU; hormonal workup was not performed at initial discovery. How does this study's findings alter your surveillance and workup approach?
items.quiz_answer: This study found that 31.7% of ACC patients had antecedent nodules indolent for a median of nearly 5 years, directly challenging the assumption that ACC lacks a detectable precursor phase. This suggests a subgroup of ACCs evolve from pre-existing lesions, extending the window for surgical cure if identified early. For this patient, complete hormonal evaluation (cortisol autonomy, pheochromocytoma, aldosterone) is essential and was inadequate in 53.6% of cases in this series. The study also found adrenal biopsy was associated with worse outcomes, reinforcing that biopsy should be avoided when ACC is a reasonable concern. Continued surveillance with attention to growth and imaging characteristics — rather than biopsy or dismissal — is appropriate.

items.title: Molecular clusters and precision medicine in pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas.
items.summary: This comprehensive review synthesizes two decades of PPGL genomics, establishing three main molecular clusters (pseudohypoxic, kinase-signaling, and Wnt-signaling) with direct therapeutic implications. Notably, FDA-approved targeted agents now exist for key driver alterations: belzutifan for HIF-2α (EPAS1/VHL pathway) and selpercatinib/pralsetinib for RET. The review also covers genomic determinants of metastatic risk—SDHB, ATRX, TERT, and MAML3 fusions—and highlights emerging theranostic, liquid biopsy, and immunotherapy approaches reshaping management of metastatic disease.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review synthesizing existing data rather than presenting new primary evidence; recommendations regarding FDA-approved agents reflect current labeling but prospective trial data specifically in PPGL for some agents remain limited.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman with a metastatic paraganglioma is found to carry a germline VHL pathogenic variant. Her tumor demonstrates HIF-2α pathway activation. Which FDA-approved targeted agent, highlighted in recent PPGL molecular cluster frameworks, would be most appropriate to consider for this patient?
items.quiz_answer: Belzutifan, a selective HIF-2α inhibitor, is FDA-approved and mechanistically targeted to the pseudohypoxic cluster driven by VHL/EPAS1 alterations. It represents a precision medicine option for metastatic PPGLs with this molecular profile.

items.title: Adrenal incidentalomas: 1 mg dexamethasone test result in the context of cardiometabolic risk.
items.summary: In this retrospective cross-sectional study of 807 adrenal incidentaloma patients, post-DST cortisol concentrations (using the standard 1 mg overnight DST) were significantly higher in patients with hypertension, coronary heart disease, heart failure, diabetes, COPD, and CKD. However, after multivariable adjustment, post-DST cortisol was not independently associated with the composite cardiometabolic endpoint; age and obesity remained the dominant predictors. An exploratory analysis suggested that cortisol levels >1.37 µg/dL—below the conventional 1.8 µg/dL cutoff—may be associated with higher cardiometabolic burden, raising questions about whether the current diagnostic threshold is optimal.
items.caveat: Retrospective, cross-sectional design precludes causal inference; the 1.37 µg/dL exploratory threshold was derived from this dataset and not pre-specified, requiring prospective validation before any clinical application. Confounding by age and obesity cannot be fully excluded.
items.quiz_question: A 68-year-old woman with an adrenal incidentaloma has a post-1 mg DST cortisol of 1.5 µg/dL—below the standard 1.8 µg/dL cutoff for MACS—but has difficult-to-control hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Based on emerging data on sub-threshold cortisol secretion and cardiometabolic risk, how should you counsel her?
items.quiz_answer: Current guidelines classify her as 'non-functioning' based on the 1.8 µg/dL cutoff. However, emerging data suggest that cortisol values between approximately 1.37 and 1.8 µg/dL may still be associated with adverse cardiometabolic profiles. At this stage, evidence is insufficient to change the diagnostic threshold; clinicians should optimize cardiovascular risk factors and consider repeat evaluation, but should not yet reclassify or intervene surgically based on sub-threshold DST cortisol alone pending prospective validation.

items.title: Corticotroph Tumour Progression 37 Years After Bilateral Adrenalectomy with Temozolomide-Naive Response to Pembrolizumab.
items.summary: This case describes corticotroph tumor progression (Nelson's syndrome equivalent) presenting 37 years after bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease—one of the latest documented presentations in the literature—underscoring the need for lifelong post-adrenalectomy surveillance. Tumor profiling revealed an aggressive molecular phenotype (ATRX loss, MEN1 inactivation, CDK4 amplification, Ki-67 10%) with absent PD-L1 expression. Pembrolizumab, given concurrently for metastatic melanoma, produced a rapid and sustained biochemical and radiological response, making this only the fifth reported case of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response in corticotrophinoma post-adrenalectomy and the first without prior temozolomide-induced hypermutation.
items.caveat: Single case report; ICI response cannot be attributed solely to pembrolizumab versus possible melanoma-related immune effects, and PD-L1 negativity raises mechanistic uncertainty. Generalizing to other corticotroph tumors requires prospective data.
items.quiz_question: A 60-year-old patient with a history of bilateral adrenalectomy for Cushing's disease 35 years ago presents with rising ACTH levels and an enlarging pituitary mass. Tumor profiling shows ATRX loss and Ki-67 of 12%. He has no prior temozolomide exposure. What emerging therapeutic approach, supported by recent case evidence, may be worth considering after standard options are exhausted?
items.quiz_answer: Immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy (e.g., pembrolizumab) has now been reported to produce biochemical and radiological responses in aggressive corticotroph tumors post-adrenalectomy, including in PD-L1-negative tumors without prior temozolomide exposure. While evidence remains at the case-report level, molecular profiling and multidisciplinary tumor board review are warranted to guide access to ICI therapy in this aggressive subtype.

items.title: Importance of clinical profiling to determine excess mortality in prolactinomas: insights from a large, registry-based cohort.
items.summary: This SEER database analysis of 3,378 adult prolactinoma cases found significant overall excess all-cause mortality (SMR 1.21) compared to the general population — a finding that challenges the widely held assumption that prolactinoma carries no mortality risk. Unsupervised clustering identified two distinct profiles: a 'LOOM' group (Large or Older, Male-predominant, 37%) with significantly elevated mortality (SMR 1.36), and a 'SAYF' group (Small and Young, Female-predominant, 63%) with directionally lower mortality. These results suggest that population-averaged reassurances about prolactinoma prognosis may obscure meaningful heterogeneity, particularly for older men with larger tumors.
items.caveat: Registry-based data lack granular clinical details (e.g., treatment type, dopamine agonist adherence, comorbidities), and the survival advantage in the SAYF group was attenuated and non-significant in sensitivity analyses with imputed data. Authors appropriately label findings as hypothesis-generating.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old man is found to have a 2.4 cm macroprolactinoma with a prolactin of 1,200 ng/mL. His primary care physician reassures him that 'prolactinomas don't affect lifespan.' Based on this registry study, how should you counsel him?
items.quiz_answer: This patient fits the higher-risk 'LOOM' profile (large tumor, older age, male sex), which was associated with significantly elevated all-cause mortality (SMR 1.36). While findings are hypothesis-generating and causal mechanisms are unclear, population-level reassurance is not appropriate for this subgroup; close follow-up addressing cardiovascular and metabolic comorbidities is warranted.

items.title: Disentangling secretory ambiguity and the limitations of classical thresholds in defining prolactinomas.
items.summary: In a surgical cohort of 425 pituitary adenoma patients, 42% of pathology-confirmed macroprolactinomas fell below the widely used 200 ng/mL diagnostic threshold, landing in the diagnostic grey zone (ULN < prolactin < 200 ng/mL) — the same zone occupied by 49% of macro-NFPAs with stalk effect. The authors introduce a Prolactin Secretory Efficiency (PSE) metric (prolactin-to-tumor volume ratio) that achieves better group separation than raw prolactin alone, though a paradox remains: high-efficiency stalk effect in some NFPAs can generate PSE values exceeding those of low-efficiency macroprolactinomas. The paper argues for cautious use of D2-agonist trials as a diagnostic probe when prolactin falls in this grey zone, to avoid misclassifying a true prolactinoma as an NFPA.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center surgical cohort; PSE calculation requires accurate volumetric tumor measurement, which varies by measurement technique. The PSE framework has not been prospectively validated, and the clinical threshold for a 'diagnostic' dopamine agonist trial response remains undefined.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man has a 2.8 cm pituitary macroadenoma and a serum prolactin of 145 ng/mL. Neurosurgery plans resection for presumed NFPA with stalk effect. What does this study suggest you consider before proceeding?
items.quiz_answer: This prolactin level falls in the grey zone (above ULN but below 200 ng/mL), and per this study, 42% of pathology-confirmed macroprolactinomas and 49% of macro-NFPAs occupy this range — making biochemical discrimination unreliable. A short trial of a D2-agonist (e.g., cabergoline) may serve as a low-risk diagnostic probe; a meaningful prolactin decline and tumor shrinkage would support prolactinoma biology and favor continued medical management over surgery.

items.title: Clinical management challenges of Cushing's disease associated with double pituitary adenomas: four cases and literature review.
items.summary: This case series and literature review (72 total patients) highlights a clinically important pitfall in Cushing's disease: double pituitary adenomas (DPAs), where a non-corticotroph adenoma is resected first and hypercortisolism persists because the true ACTH-secreting lesion is missed. In all four institutional cases, initial TSS removed a non-corticotroph adenoma; the corticotroph adenoma was identified on repeat imaging (including 68Ga-pentixafor PET/CT in two cases with equivocal MRI) and confirmed at revision surgery, with all four achieving biochemical remission. Across the combined cohort, preoperative MRI identified both lesions in only 17% of cases, underscoring the diagnostic challenge.
items.caveat: Combined cohort is heterogeneous with variable reporting quality across 30 publications spanning 35 years; 68Ga-pentixafor PET/CT data are preliminary and drawn from only two cases. The true prevalence of DPAs in Cushing's disease is unknown.
items.quiz_question: A 34-year-old woman undergoes TSS for Cushing's disease. Pathology shows a null-cell adenoma with no ACTH or T-PIT immunoreactivity. Her postoperative UFC remains elevated. What should be the next step in her evaluation?
items.quiz_answer: Persistent hypercortisolism after resection of a non-corticotroph adenoma should raise strong suspicion for a double pituitary adenoma with an unresected corticotroph component. Multidisciplinary re-review of imaging is essential; if MRI is equivocal, 68Ga-pentixafor PET/CT may help localize a second lesion. Repeat expert TSS targeting the ACTH-secreting adenoma is the definitive treatment.

items.title: Clinical presentation, investigation findings, and outcomes of hypophysitis in sarcoidosis: a systematic review.
items.summary: This systematic review of 274 patients with sarcoidosis-related hypophysitis found that AVP (arginine vasopressin) deficiency was the most common manifestation (54%), followed by gonadal dysfunction and visual loss. Despite corticosteroid treatment being the mainstay, recurrence occurred in 43% and chronic hormone replacement was required in 36%, with desmopressin dependence persisting in 31%. MRI most commonly showed pituitary stalk thickening and sellar/suprasellar masses, while serum and CSF biomarkers had limited sensitivity, underscoring the need for systemic investigation and extracranial biopsy for diagnosis.
items.caveat: The cohort spans over 70 years of publications with significant temporal heterogeneity in diagnostic criteria and treatment approaches; retrospective case-report aggregation introduces ascertainment bias, and diagnostic certainty was only 'definite' in 26% of cases.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old man with known pulmonary sarcoidosis presents with polyuria, polydipsia, and new-onset fatigue. MRI shows pituitary stalk thickening without a discrete mass. CSF protein is elevated. What is the most common anterior pituitary abnormality you should screen for in this setting, and what is the expected recurrence rate of hypophysitis despite corticosteroid treatment?
items.quiz_answer: Central hypogonadism is the most common anterior pituitary abnormality (74%), followed by central hypothyroidism (64%) and hyperprolactinemia (58%). Despite corticosteroid treatment, recurrence occurs in approximately 43% of patients, and long-term hormone replacement is required in about 36%, highlighting the need for sustained multidisciplinary follow-up.

items.title: Natural history of conservatively managed nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenomas in the elderly: A study from the Swedish Pituitary Registry.
items.summary: In this large registry study of 673 patients ≥65 years with nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenomas managed conservatively, adenoma size, hormone deficiencies, and visual impairments remained stable over up to 5 years of follow-up in all age subgroups. Only 6.7% required surgery during follow-up, and baseline visual field defects—not tumor size—were the sole predictor of eventual surgical intervention. These data support a watchful-waiting approach in elderly patients without visual compromise.
items.caveat: Registry-based retrospective design with incomplete follow-up data at 5 years; selection bias is likely since patients chosen for conservative management may inherently have more indolent tumors; survival effects in the oldest age groups could mask tumor progression.
items.quiz_question: A 78-year-old man is found to have a 22-mm nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma on incidental MRI. He has no visual symptoms and mild secondary hypogonadism. His neurosurgeon asks whether tumor size alone should prompt surgery. Based on the Swedish Pituitary Registry data, what factor best predicts need for eventual surgery in elderly patients managed conservatively?
items.quiz_answer: Baseline visual field defects—not tumor size—were the only significant predictor of later surgical intervention in this cohort. Tumor size, hormone deficiencies, and visual acuity did not independently predict surgery, supporting conservative management with regular surveillance in elderly patients without visual compromise.

items.title: Unrecognized primary aldosteronism may confound outcomes in adrenal Cushing's syndrome.
items.summary: This letter highlights a clinically important gap: in a Colombian registry of 130 patients with adrenal Cushing's syndrome, none of the 22 patients were screened for primary aldosteronism (PA) prior to adrenalectomy, despite current guideline recommendations. Because hypertension and hypokalemia are shared features of both conditions, postoperative complications and persistent hypertension may be misattributed to cortisol excess alone when co-secretion of aldosterone goes undetected. The authors call for routine PA screening in adrenal Cushing's patients with hypertension.
items.caveat: This is a brief letter/correspondence based on a single-center registry with a small subgroup (n=22); it demonstrates a care gap but does not provide outcome data on whether missed PA actually changed postoperative results in these patients.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old woman with a 3.5-cm right adrenal adenoma undergoes evaluation for adrenal Cushing's syndrome. Post-1-mg dexamethasone suppression test cortisol is 6.2 µg/dL; she also has resistant hypertension and hypokalemia requiring supplementation. Her endocrinologist plans adrenalectomy. What additional screening step do current guidelines recommend before surgery, and why is it particularly important in this clinical context?
items.quiz_answer: Current guidelines recommend screening for primary aldosteronism (aldosterone-to-renin ratio) in adrenal Cushing's syndrome patients with hypertension. Co-secretion of aldosterone may occur from the same adenoma, and failure to diagnose PA preoperatively can lead to persistent hypokalemia and hypertension postoperatively that is incorrectly attributed to incomplete resolution of hypercortisolism rather than to ongoing aldosterone excess.
items.journal: Therapeutic advances in endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Approach to the Patient: Diagnosis and Management of Cushing's Syndrome in the Elderly - How Different Is It?
items.summary: This JCEM clinical guidance piece addresses the underappreciated diagnostic and therapeutic nuances of Cushing's syndrome in older adults, who often lack classic cushingoid features and instead present with poorly controlled diabetes/hypertension, falls, rapid bone loss, proximal weakness, VTE, cognitive decline, or adrenal incidentaloma. The authors provide a practical framework for test selection that accounts for renal function, sleep disturbance, drug interactions, and the elevated pre-test probability of non-neoplastic hypercortisolism in this age group — noting that LNSC should be repeated and interpreted cautiously in patients with diabetes or acute illness, and that UFC may be falsely low in CKD. Importantly, the paper advocates that fit older adults should receive standard curative therapy, while frail patients may benefit from staged or symptom-directed approaches with explicit goals around preserving mobility, cognition, and independence.
items.caveat: This is a narrative/opinion-style 'Approach to the Patient' piece rather than an original research study; recommendations are expert-derived and not supported by prospective trials specifically in elderly Cushing's populations.
items.quiz_question: A 74-year-old woman with CKD stage 3, poorly controlled hypertension, and recent fragility fracture is referred for evaluation of possible Cushing's syndrome. She has no classic cushingoid features. Which screening test would you interpret with the most caution in this patient, and why?
items.quiz_answer: Urinary free cortisol (UFC) should be interpreted with the most caution, as it may be falsely low in chronic kidney disease due to reduced renal excretion. Late-night salivary cortisol and the 1-mg dexamethasone suppression test (with attention to drug interactions and dexamethasone levels if needed) are preferred initial screening tools in this population, per the paper's guidance.
items.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Hounsfield unit thresholds in differentiating adenoma from nonadenoma adrenal masses: a retrospective adrenalectomy-based study.
items.summary: This retrospective study of 106 adrenalectomy patients compared Hounsfield unit (HU) thresholds on non-contrast CT for distinguishing adrenal adenomas from non-adenomas (malignancies, metastases, pheochromocytomas). ROC analysis identified 20 HU as the optimal threshold by Youden's index, yielding sensitivity/specificity of 92%/82%, substantially improving specificity over the conventional 10 HU cutoff (98%/56%) while maintaining clinically acceptable sensitivity. Mean HU values were 11.4 for adenomas versus 35.9 for non-adenomas, and lesion size was also significantly larger in non-adenomas (55.8 vs. 37.2 mm).
items.caveat: Critical limitation: this is a selected adrenalectomy cohort, not an unselected incidentaloma population — surgical cases are enriched for non-adenomas, which inflates specificity estimates for any threshold. The authors appropriately call for prospective validation before guideline revision. Adopting 20 HU in routine practice could miss lipid-rich adenomas if sensitivity drops in broader populations.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman has a 3.2 cm right adrenal incidentaloma with a non-contrast CT attenuation of 14 HU. Using the conventional 10 HU threshold she clears as likely adenoma, but a colleague argues for 20 HU based on new data. What is the key limitation of applying the 20 HU cutoff from this study to her clinical management?
items.quiz_answer: The 20 HU threshold was derived from a surgical (adrenalectomy) cohort enriched for non-adenomas, not from an unselected incidentaloma population. In lower-prevalence settings like routine incidentaloma evaluation, the specificity benefit may not replicate and sensitivity could be insufficient, risking misclassification of lipid-rich adenomas. The authors themselves caution against changing clinical guidelines until prospective validation in unselected incidentaloma populations is performed.

items.title: Synergistic prognostic value of transcription factor multiplicity and Ki-67 in pituitary neuroendocrine tumour recurrence after endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery: a novel tiered molecular risk model.
items.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 302 patients undergoing primary endoscopic transsphenoidal surgery for PitNETs, this study demonstrates that combining lineage-defining transcription factor (TF) multiplicity with Ki-67 provides superior recurrence prediction compared to either marker alone. A 4-tiered molecular risk model was developed: at the highest tier (multiple TF positivity + Ki-67 ≥3%), adjusted hazard ratios for recurrence reached 15–18-fold compared to the lowest-risk tier, far exceeding the HR of ~1.76 for Ki-67 alone. Importantly, the authors also validated a simplified version using unspecific TF multiplicity (any co-expression) plus Ki-67, making it applicable across pathology labs with varying immunohistochemical capabilities.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with median follow-up of only 30 months; 26.8% recurrence rate at this follow-up window may underestimate long-term events. The tiered model requires external multicenter validation before it can guide post-operative surveillance intervals in routine practice.
items.quiz_question: You receive a pathology report on a surgically resected non-functioning PitNET showing co-expression of SF-1 and T-PIT (dual TF positivity) with Ki-67 of 5%. Based on this study's tiered molecular risk model, how should this inform your post-operative management compared to a single-TF, Ki-67 <3% tumor?
items.quiz_answer: This tumor would fall into a high-risk tier (multiple TF positivity combined with elevated Ki-67 ≥3%), associated with adjusted hazard ratios for recurrence of approximately 6.5–17-fold compared to the lowest-risk group. This should prompt earlier and more frequent post-operative MRI surveillance compared to a single-TF, low Ki-67 tumor, and may support discussion of adjuvant radiosurgery — though the specific surveillance protocol should await external validation of this model.

items.title: Tumor Necrosis is Associated with an Increased Metastatic and Cardiovascular Risk in Paragangliomas: A Single-Center Series and Meta-Analysis Comparing Necrosis and Cystic Degeneration in Paragangliomas.
items.summary: In a retrospective series of 103 PGL patients plus a meta-analysis of 235 additional cases, necrotic alterations (present in ~4% of PGLs) were independently associated with a dramatically higher metastasis rate (75% vs. 10% in the single-center cohort; 16% vs. 4.5% in the meta-analysis) and significantly more cardiovascular complications. Cystic alterations, by contrast—seen in over 60% of PGLs—did not meaningfully alter clinical presentation or outcomes. Necrotic PGLs also tended to be much larger (median 53.6 vs. 6.6 cm³) and more symptomatic. The practical implication is that the histopathologic distinction between cystic and necrotic change on imaging or pathology reports should actively inform risk stratification, preoperative workup intensity, and post-resection surveillance intervals.
items.caveat: Necrotic PGLs represented only 3.9% of the single-center series (n≈4), so the 75% metastasis rate derives from a very small numerator; the meta-analysis pool (235 patients) is also modest and likely heterogeneous across centers and era. Retrospective design limits causal inference.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old patient with a 6 cm adrenal paraganglioma undergoes pathologic evaluation after adrenalectomy. The pathologist notes areas of tumor necrosis. How should this finding alter your post-surgical management compared to a PGL with only cystic degeneration?
items.quiz_answer: Necrotic change—unlike cystic degeneration—is associated with substantially higher rates of metastasis (~16–75% vs. ~4–10%) and cardiovascular complications. This finding should prompt more intensive and prolonged surveillance (e.g., shorter imaging intervals, functional imaging consideration) and a lower threshold for evaluating for metastatic disease, whereas cystic-only changes do not appear to confer additional risk beyond the baseline PGL.

items.title: Specialist consultation improves underdiagnosis of surgical adrenal incidentaloma: a TriNetX database investigation.
items.summary: In a large real-world TriNetX database analysis of 132,217 patients with adrenal incidentalomas, only 0.7% received any specialist consultation, yet specialist referral nearly doubled the rate of hormonal testing (49.5% vs. 28.0%) and significantly increased surgical rates (6.3% vs. 3.6%). Crucially, once hormonal testing occurred, surgery rates were identical regardless of specialist involvement (~13%), suggesting the bottleneck is getting patients to evaluation—not decision-making at the specialist level. Extrapolating the ~13% surgery rate to all undertested patients implies roughly 14,000 patients in this database likely met surgical criteria but never received the workup to identify it.
items.caveat: TriNetX is a claims/EHR network subject to coding inaccuracies and selection bias; 'specialist consultation' was broadly defined and may include urologists or surgeons who may not perform full endocrine evaluation. Causality cannot be established—sicker or higher-complexity patients may have been preferentially referred.
items.quiz_question: A primary care physician discovers a 3.2 cm adrenal mass on CT obtained for an unrelated indication in a 61-year-old hypertensive woman. She is not referred to endocrinology. Based on the TriNetX data, what is the most likely gap in her care, and what proportion of such patients may be missing a surgical indication?
items.quiz_answer: Without specialist referral, only ~28% of incidentaloma patients receive any hormonal testing vs. ~50% with referral. Since ~13% of those who are hormonally tested ultimately require surgery, and the vast majority of incidentaloma patients never get tested, approximately 13% of all incidentaloma patients may have a missed surgical indication—translating to thousands of patients nationally who are undertreated.

items.title: Prevalence of sick leave before and after pituitary adenoma surgery.
items.summary: This Swedish registry study of 66 working-age patients who underwent transsphenoidal surgery (TSS) for pituitary adenoma found that sickness compensation rates were approximately double those of matched population controls in the year before surgery, continued to rise up to the time of surgery, and declined thereafter but remained elevated at 1 year post-op—never returning to pre-diagnosis levels. Among patients who failed to return to work by 1 year, greater fatigue burden and adrenal insufficiency were significantly more common, and Cushing's disease (though a small subgroup) predicted more days to return to work. These findings highlight that work disability is a persistent, real-world outcome that extends well beyond the perioperative period and deserves routine attention in long-term pituitary care.
items.caveat: Small cohort (n=66) from a single Swedish center limits generalizability; the Cushing's disease subgroup was too small for definitive inference. Observational design precludes establishing causality between specific complications (e.g., adrenal insufficiency) and work disability.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old accountant undergoes successful TSS for a non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma and develops post-operative adrenal insufficiency requiring hydrocortisone replacement. She reports persistent fatigue at her 6-month follow-up and has not returned to work. How does this Swedish registry study inform your counseling and management?
items.quiz_answer: The study found that patients who had not returned to work by 1 year post-TSS reported significantly more fatigue and were more likely to have adrenal insufficiency than those who did return. This supports proactive screening for undertreated adrenal insufficiency, optimization of hydrocortisone dosing, and formal fatigue assessment in patients struggling to resume work—with realistic counseling that sickness compensation often remains elevated beyond the surgical period.

items.title: Use of osilodrostat in a block-and-replace and titration strategy for cushing's syndrome: a position paper by French experts.
items.summary: A group of French experts published a consensus position statement on the block-and-replace (B&R) strategy using osilodrostat for Cushing's syndrome, arguing it is a viable alternative to standard gradual titration in selected patients—particularly when rapid disease control is needed in severe cases or when frequent monitoring is logistically challenging. The authors acknowledge that B&R avoids the delays and cortisol fluctuations inherent to titration, but emphasize this is expert opinion rather than guideline-level evidence. They call for randomized controlled trials directly comparing the two strategies across diverse populations before broader adoption.
items.caveat: This is an expert-driven position paper, not evidence-based from RCT data; there is no head-to-head trial comparing B&R vs. titration with osilodrostat, and the patient selection criteria for B&R remain incompletely defined.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old woman with severe ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease (UFC >10x ULN, uncontrolled hypertension, poorly controlled diabetes) has had unsuccessful transsphenoidal surgery and is not yet a candidate for repeat surgery or radiation. You initiate osilodrostat. According to the French expert position statement, in which clinical scenario might a block-and-replace strategy be preferred over standard gradual titration?
items.quiz_answer: The block-and-replace strategy is preferred when rapid disease control is imperative (e.g., severe hypercortisolism with life-threatening complications) or when the logistical demands of frequent monitoring for titration are not feasible. In this patient with severe, refractory disease, B&R with osilodrostat plus physiologic glucocorticoid replacement may achieve eucortisolism more quickly than stepwise titration, though this approach requires careful patient selection and remains expert opinion pending RCT confirmation.

items.title: Metyrapone in the Management of Severe Hypercortisolism Secondary to Ectopic Cushing's Syndrome.
items.summary: This case series describes three patients with severe hypercortisolism from ectopic ACTH syndrome (neuroendocrine carcinoma, NSCLC-related metastatic NEC, and metastatic prostate cancer) all managed successfully with rapid metyrapone titration. Biochemical control was achieved in all three using initial doses of 1000–1500 mg/day in divided doses alongside physiologic glucocorticoid replacement to prevent adrenal insufficiency. Despite cortisol normalization and metabolic stabilization, all three patients ultimately transitioned to comfort-focused care, reflecting the aggressive natural history of these underlying malignancies.
items.caveat: Only three cases; conclusions on dosing and titration strategy are limited by small sample size and heterogeneous underlying etiologies. The paper acknowledges that the rarity and aggressiveness of ectopic CS make standardized guidance difficult to derive.
items.quiz_question: A 64-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer presents with hypokalemia, uncontrolled hypertension, hyperglycemia, and a 24-hour UFC of 18x ULN, consistent with ectopic ACTH syndrome. You initiate metyrapone. Based on this case series, what starting dose and key co-treatment should you employ to minimize the risk of adrenal insufficiency?
items.quiz_answer: Based on the reported experience, an initial metyrapone dose of 1000–1500 mg/day in divided doses is recommended, with concurrent physiologic glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., hydrocortisone) to mitigate the risk of adrenal insufficiency caused by 11-β hydroxylase blockade. Close biochemical monitoring is essential given the rapid cortisol lowering typical of ectopic CS.

items.title: Differences in management and outcomes between pheochromocytomas and sympathetic paragangliomas.
items.summary: This retrospective study of 220 patients at a single academic center found that sympathetic paragangliomas (PGL) had notably worse long-term outcomes compared to pheochromocytomas (PCC): PGL patients had longer hospital stays (7 vs. 4 days), and significantly higher rates of new related tumors—including recurrence, metastasis, or metachronous tumor—during follow-up (27.8% vs. 11.0%, p=0.019). PCC patients more frequently presented with dysglycemia (42.2% vs. 17.6%), which also improved more often after surgery. Preoperative alpha-blockade duration was longer for PCC (50 vs. 34 days).
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design over 20 years introduces heterogeneity in management protocols and follow-up duration; differences in tumor size, genetic background, and imaging surveillance intensity between PCC and PGL groups were not fully adjusted for.
items.quiz_question: A 38-year-old woman is found to have a 4 cm retroperitoneal sympathetic paraganglioma. She asks about her long-term prognosis compared to a patient with a similarly sized adrenal pheochromocytoma. Based on this study, what key difference in long-term oncologic outcomes should you convey?
items.quiz_answer: Sympathetic paraganglioma patients face a significantly higher risk of new related tumors (recurrence, metastasis, or metachronous tumor) during follow-up compared to pheochromocytoma patients (27.8% vs. 11.0%). This underscores the importance of long-term surveillance imaging and biochemical testing in PGL, and reinforces current guideline recommendations for more intensive follow-up in paraganglioma versus adrenal PCC.

items.title: Clinical and pharmacological determinants of serum dexamethasone concentrations during dexamethasone suppression test.
items.summary: In this observational study of 546 patients undergoing the 1-mg overnight DST with simultaneous serum dexamethasone measurement, older age and higher BMI were independently associated with higher dexamethasone exposure in multivariable analysis, while eGFR had no significant independent effect. Suboptimal dexamethasone exposure (<4.5 nmol/L) occurred in 3.3% of patients and was frequently associated with failure to suppress cortisol, underscoring the value of concurrent dexamethasone measurement. Importantly, once adequate dexamethasone exposure was achieved, higher dexamethasone levels did not produce additional cortisol suppression — suggesting a ceiling effect rather than a dose-dependent relationship across the therapeutic range.
items.caveat: Observational single-center design limits causal inference; medication associations (PPIs, statins, CCBs) did not survive all sensitivity analyses, so their clinical significance remains uncertain. Patients with mild autonomous cortisol secretion were included, potentially confounding cortisol suppression results.
items.quiz_question: A 72-year-old man with BMI 34 kg/m² undergoes a 1-mg overnight DST; his serum cortisol is 3.1 µg/dL. You are uncertain whether this represents true hypercortisolism or suboptimal dexamethasone absorption. Based on this study's findings, what single additional measurement would most efficiently clarify interpretation, and what patient characteristics in this case predict his dexamethasone exposure?
items.quiz_answer: Measuring a simultaneous serum dexamethasone level is the key additional test. This study shows that older age and higher BMI are independently associated with *higher* (not lower) dexamethasone exposure, so this patient's profile would actually predict adequate or above-average exposure. If dexamethasone is confirmed adequate (≥4.5 nmol/L), the cortisol of 3.1 µg/dL (above the 1.8 µg/dL cutoff) supports further evaluation for mild autonomous cortisol secretion rather than attributing the result to pharmacokinetic failure.
items.journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism

items.title: Comparison of Cardiometabolic Profiles in Patients with Nonfunctioning Adrenal Incidentalomas and Mild Autonomous Cortisol Secretion.
items.summary: This retrospective study of 67 patients compared MACS (post-1-mg DST cortisol ≥1.8 µg/dL, n=35) versus NFAI (n=32) and found that MACS patients had significantly lower ACTH, lower DHEA-S, and higher triglycerides — consistent with subtle but real glucocorticoid excess. Despite these metabolic differences, global longitudinal strain (GLS) on echocardiography did not differ significantly between groups, and nominal correlations between GLS and cortisol-related biochemical parameters did not survive false discovery rate correction. The absence of detectable subclinical myocardial dysfunction by GLS in a cross-sectional design does not exclude longer-term cardiovascular risk from MACS.
items.caveat: Small sample size (n=67) substantially limits statistical power to detect GLS differences; the cross-sectional design precludes any causal inference about MACS and cardiac outcomes. The study was not powered as a cardiovascular outcomes trial and should not be interpreted as reassuring evidence that MACS carries no cardiac risk.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with a 2.2-cm right adrenal incidentaloma has a post-1-mg DST cortisol of 3.2 µg/dL, ACTH of 9 pg/mL, DHEA-S in the low-normal range, and triglycerides of 210 mg/dL. Her echocardiogram shows normal ejection fraction. How does this study inform your discussion of cardiovascular risk with her, and what management approach does it support?
items.quiz_answer: This study confirms the MACS biochemical phenotype (suppressed ACTH, low DHEA-S, elevated triglycerides) she demonstrates, and shows that conventional echo including GLS may not capture early myocardial changes in cross-sectional assessment. The absence of a GLS difference should not be interpreted as cardiac safety reassurance. Per current guidance, her cardiometabolic comorbidities (hypertriglyceridemia) should be actively managed, and longitudinal surveillance for progressive cortisol autonomy and cardiovascular risk factors is warranted.

items.title: Endoscopic endonasal transcavernous surgery for knosp grade 3-4 growth hormone-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumors: surgical outcomes and predictors of biochemical remission.
items.summary: This retrospective single-center study of 50 patients with Knosp grade 3–4 GH-PitNETs compared outcomes before and after adoption of an endoscopic endonasal transcavernous approach (transcavernous-EEA). The biochemical remission rate was significantly higher in the transcavernous-EEA group (64.7% vs. 31.3%, p=0.027), without increased surgical morbidity. In exploratory multivariable analysis of the transcavernous-EEA cohort, lower preoperative IGF-1 (cutoff ~587 ng/mL) and lower day-1 postoperative GH (cutoff ~2.2 ng/mL, AUC 0.898) were independently associated with remission, suggesting POD1 GH may serve as an early remission predictor even in this invasive subgroup.
items.caveat: Retrospective single-center design with only 17 patients in the transcavernous-EEA group; historical controls introduce substantial confounding from evolving surgical technique and case selection. Cutoff values are preliminary and exploratory, not validated in an independent cohort. Follow-up duration is not clearly specified for remission assessment.
items.quiz_question: A 41-year-old man with acromegaly and a Knosp grade 4 macroadenoma has a preoperative IGF-1 of 520 ng/mL. On postoperative day 1, his random GH is 1.8 ng/mL. Based on this study's findings, how would you characterize his likelihood of biochemical remission, and what would be your next management step?
items.quiz_answer: Both his preoperative IGF-1 (<587 ng/mL threshold) and POD1 GH (<2.185 ng/mL cutoff, AUC 0.898) fall within the range independently associated with biochemical remission in the transcavernous-EEA cohort of this study. These are favorable early indicators. The next step is formal IGF-1 measurement at 3 months postoperatively to confirm remission, with continued assessment for hypopituitarism, and a plan for adjuvant medical therapy (somatostatin receptor ligand or pegvisomant) if remission is not confirmed biochemically.

items.title: A long-acting octreotide analog formed by conjugation with a peptide linker modified with two fatty acids.
items.summary: TE-8214 is a depot-free, aqueous-formulated octreotide analog designed to bind human serum albumin, extending its half-life without the need for large-bore needle depot injections. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 1 single-ascending-dose study in healthy adults (0.6–4.0 mg), TE-8214 was well-tolerated with no serious or Grade ≥3 adverse events, and produced sustained, dose-dependent IGF-1 suppression lasting through Day 28 at the highest dose tested. Preclinical studies in rodents and dogs confirmed prolonged GH, IGF-1, and serotonin suppression exceeding equimolar octreotide, supporting the albumin-binding mechanism.
items.caveat: This was a Phase 1 study in healthy volunteers, not patients with acromegaly or NETs; therapeutic efficacy remains unproven and the IGF-1 reduction (22.5% at highest dose) was an exploratory endpoint. Industry sponsorship and small sample size limit generalizability.
items.quiz_question: A 48-year-old patient with acromegaly currently managed with monthly intramuscular octreotide LAR injections reports significant injection-site pain and nodularity. A novel depot-free somatostatin analog (TE-8214) has completed Phase 1 testing. What is the mechanism by which this agent achieves prolonged action without a depot formulation, and what Phase 1 pharmacodynamic finding supports its potential clinical utility?
items.quiz_answer: TE-8214 achieves prolonged systemic exposure by conjugating octreotide to a dual-fatty-acid albumin-binding module, enabling reversible binding to human serum albumin and extending the terminal half-life. In the Phase 1 trial, a single subcutaneous dose (via 30-gauge needle) produced a sustained 22.5% reduction in IGF-1 from baseline that persisted through Day 28, demonstrating clinically meaningful pharmacodynamic activity over a month following one injection.

items.title: Adrenal Suppression From Mucosal Absorption of Dexamethasone Mouthwash.
items.summary: This case report describes a breast cancer patient on immunotherapy who developed secondary adrenal insufficiency attributable to systemic absorption of a dexamethasone mouthwash used strictly as 'swish and spit' without swallowing, confirmed by elevated serum dexamethasone levels. The key clinical implication is that ICI-related hypophysitis/adrenal insufficiency is often presumed permanent and treated lifelong, but this case illustrates a reversible, drug-induced mimic that would be managed very differently. Recognizing occult topical glucocorticoid exposure—including oral mucosal routes—is essential before committing an oncology patient to lifelong adrenal replacement.
items.caveat: Single case report; prevalence of clinically significant mucosal dexamethasone absorption in oncology patients is unknown and likely underreported. No formal pharmacokinetic data on mouthwash absorption are provided in the abstract.
items.quiz_question: A 62-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer on pembrolizumab develops fatigue and a low morning cortisol with suppressed ACTH. She is diagnosed with presumed ICI-induced adrenal insufficiency and started on hydrocortisone replacement. Before committing her to lifelong therapy, what additional medication history inquiry is critical, and why?
items.quiz_answer: Clinicians should specifically ask about use of dexamethasone mouthwash (commonly prescribed for oral mucositis in oncology patients), even if used as 'swish and spit.' Systemic mucosal absorption can suppress the HPA axis and mimic ICI-induced adrenal insufficiency; confirming elevated serum dexamethasone would identify a reversible cause, sparing the patient from unnecessary lifelong glucocorticoid replacement.

items.title: Diagnostic Challenge of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-Induced Hypophysitis in Patient With Melanoma.
items.summary: This case describes a 73-year-old man with metastatic melanoma who developed ICI-induced hypophysitis after combination ipilimumab/nivolumab therapy, presenting with fatigue, headache, and hyponatremia driven by central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency confirmed on cosyntropin stimulation testing. Pituitary MRI showed gland enlargement, and normal adrenal imaging excluded metastatic disease. The report reinforces that ICI-induced hypophysitis is typically irreversible, requiring ongoing hormone replacement, and that the diagnostic presentation can closely mimic other conditions—making a structured endocrine evaluation protocol essential as ICI use expands broadly across oncology.
items.caveat: Single case report from a VA center; the relative incidence of hypophysitis with anti-PD-1 monotherapy vs. combination CTLA-4/PD-1 blockade is not quantified here. The case did not detail long-term pituitary recovery data.
items.quiz_question: A 68-year-old man with metastatic melanoma presents with fatigue and sodium of 128 mEq/L after his third cycle of ipilimumab plus nivolumab. TSH is undetectable with low free T4; morning cortisol is 4 µg/dL; ACTH is low. MRI shows a mildly enlarged pituitary. CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis shows no adrenal metastases. What is the diagnosis, what is the appropriate initial treatment sequence, and what should the patient be counseled regarding long-term hormone requirements?
items.quiz_answer: The diagnosis is ICI-induced hypophysitis causing central hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency. Glucocorticoid replacement (e.g., IV hydrocortisone) should be initiated first before levothyroxine to avoid precipitating an adrenal crisis. The patient should be counseled that ICI-induced hypophysitis is generally irreversible, and lifelong hormone replacement therapy is typically required.
items.journal: Federal practitioner : for the health care professionals of the VA, DoD, and PHS

items.title: Hypercortisolism: An Under-Recognised Pathway Linked to Multi-System Complications.
items.summary: This review argues that hypercortisolism exists on a spectrum extending well beyond classic Cushing's syndrome to include mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS), which is increasingly recognized as a contributor to difficult-to-control diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, and neuropsychiatric morbidity. The authors highlight emerging data suggesting MACS may be identifiable in over 20% of high-risk individuals (e.g., resistant hypertension or poorly controlled diabetes) using standard screening tests. The review makes the practical case that earlier recognition of MACS in patients with common multimorbidity could prompt targeted evaluation and modify management strategies.
items.caveat: This is a narrative review without systematic methods or meta-analytic rigor; the cited '>20%' prevalence figure in high-risk populations requires confirmation in prospective, well-designed cohorts before changing routine screening practice.
items.quiz_question: A 58-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and resistant hypertension on four agents presents for endocrine consultation. She has no classic cushingoid features. Based on emerging data discussed in this review, what is the next appropriate diagnostic consideration, and what simple test could be used?
items.quiz_answer: Mild autonomous cortisol secretion (MACS) should be considered. A 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a well-established, readily available screening tool that can be performed in most clinical settings to evaluate for subtle cortisol excess in this high-risk phenotype.

items.title: Long-term endocrine outcomes of transsphenoidal surgery for prolactinomas: a 20-year single-center cohort study.
items.summary: This 20-year retrospective cohort study of 55 selected patients undergoing transsphenoidal surgery for prolactinomas found biochemical remission at 6 months in 53% overall—60% for microprolactinomas and 44% for macroprolactinomas—with a low long-term recurrence rate of 9%. Notably, no male patient achieved remission; however, the authors appropriately flag that men disproportionately harbored larger tumors with much higher preoperative prolactin levels, confounding any sex-based inference. Permanent surgical complications were uncommon, supporting a role for surgery as a viable second-line option in selected patients.
items.caveat: Single-center, retrospective, descriptive design with a highly selected surgical cohort limits generalizability and precludes conclusions about comparative effectiveness versus dopamine agonist therapy. The sex-based remission difference is exploratory and confounded by tumor size and prolactin levels.
items.quiz_question: A 28-year-old woman with a 12 mm microprolactinoma has intolerable side effects on both cabergoline and bromocriptine and requests surgical consultation. Based on this 20-year cohort study, what remission rate should she be counseled about for transsphenoidal surgery for microprolactinoma, and what is the long-term recurrence rate?
items.quiz_answer: In this cohort, transsphenoidal surgery for microprolactinomas achieved biochemical remission in approximately 60% of patients at 6 months, with an overall recurrence rate of 9% during a median follow-up of nearly 11 years. She should understand these are outcomes from a selected, experienced-center cohort and may not reflect results universally.

items.title: Functioning pituitary adenomas in pregnancy: updates and controversies.
items.summary: This update reviews the evolving management of prolactinomas, acromegaly, and Cushing's disease during pregnancy, synthesizing recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses. For prolactinomas, both cabergoline and bromocriptine have demonstrated consistent maternal and fetal safety profiles across studies, and surgical outcomes at specialized centers have become favorable enough that surgery is increasingly discussed as an alternative to lifelong dopamine agonist therapy for selected patients. For acromegaly and Cushing's disease in pregnancy, new medical therapies exist but pregnancy safety data remain absent, keeping management highly individualized with shared decision-making as the cornerstone.
items.caveat: The evidence base is largely retrospective given the rarity of these conditions in pregnancy; no randomized trial data exist. Guidance for acromegaly and Cushing's disease in pregnancy remains particularly limited and cannot support firm recommendations.
items.quiz_question: A 32-year-old woman with a macroprolactinoma on cabergoline is planning pregnancy and asks whether she must switch to bromocriptine, which she previously tolerated poorly, or whether cabergoline can be continued. What does the current evidence base support?
items.quiz_answer: Recent systematic reviews have demonstrated that cabergoline has an overall maternal and fetal safety profile comparable to bromocriptine. While bromocriptine has a longer safety track record, current evidence supports cabergoline as a reasonable option in selected patients, particularly when bromocriptine is not tolerated, with management individualized through shared decision-making.
items.journal: Current opinion in endocrinology, diabetes, and obesity

items.title: Preoperative Metyrosine Administration for Bilateral Pheochromocytomas Following Pheochromocytoma Crisis: A Case Report.
items.summary: A 46-year-old man with bilateral pheochromocytomas complicated by reverse Takotsubo cardiomyopathy underwent one-stage bilateral adrenalectomy after preoperative preparation with metyrosine added to conventional alpha-adrenergic blockade. Urinary metanephrines fell approximately 76% with metyrosine, and bilateral adrenalectomy was completed successfully despite residual intraoperative hemodynamic fluctuations. The case is clinically timely given metyrosine's recent approval in Japan for perioperative pheochromocytoma management, extending the evidence base for its use as an adjunct to alpha-blockade in the highest-risk patients (crisis, severe cardiomyopathy, bilateral disease). The authors appropriately note that the contribution of metyrosine to intraoperative hemodynamic stability versus alpha-blockade alone remains uncertain from this single case.
items.caveat: Single case report; no comparator arm, so the incremental benefit of metyrosine over alpha-blockade alone cannot be quantified. Metyrosine is not universally approved or available outside Japan.
items.quiz_question: A 52-year-old man with bilateral pheochromocytomas and a recent episode of catecholamine-induced cardiomyopathy (EF 25%) is being prepared for bilateral adrenalectomy. Standard alpha-blockade has been initiated. What additional pharmacologic adjunct, and through what mechanism, might be considered to further reduce perioperative catecholamine burden in this high-risk patient?
items.quiz_answer: Metyrosine (alpha-methyl-p-tyrosine) inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting enzyme in catecholamine biosynthesis, thereby reducing catecholamine synthesis and circulating metanephrine levels. In this case report, adding metyrosine to alpha-blockade reduced urinary metanephrines by ~76%, supporting its use as an adjunct in patients with preceding crisis, severe cardiac dysfunction, marked catecholamine excess, and bilateral disease.

items.title: Internal validation of THINKERS-PA for outcome prediction after pituitary adenoma radiosurgery.
items.summary: THINKERS-PA is a mixture-of-experts neural network trained on 125 patients with pituitary adenomas treated with Gamma Knife radiosurgery, predicting tumor progression, biochemical remission, and new hypopituitarism using pretreatment clinical, anatomical, and dosimetric variables. Internal cross-validation yielded time-dependent AUCs of 0.82, 0.84, and 0.81 for the three endpoints respectively, with reasonable calibration. A dose-sweeping module estimated delivered dose within ±1 Gy in 71% of patients, suggesting potential utility for pre-procedure dose optimization. The framework is methodologically interesting but requires external multicenter validation before it influences radiosurgery practice.
items.caveat: Single-center retrospective cohort of only 125 patients; internal-only validation with no external dataset. The dose-sweeping module cannot be interpreted as prospective dose guidance. Industry or institutional conflicts of interest are not reported in the abstract.
items.quiz_question: After reviewing THINKERS-PA, a colleague asks whether this tool can now be used to individualize Gamma Knife doses for pituitary adenoma patients at your institution. What is the appropriate response based on the study's current validation status?
items.quiz_answer: Not yet. THINKERS-PA has undergone only internal cross-validation in a single-center retrospective cohort of 125 patients. The authors explicitly state that external multicenter validation is required before clinical implementation. Promising AUCs (0.81–0.84) justify further study, but the tool should not guide clinical dosing decisions until prospectively validated in independent cohorts.

items.title: Association between preoperative MRI radiomic features and methylation-defined phenotypes in non-functioning pituitary adenomas.
items.summary: In a single-center radiogenomic analysis of 74 patients with non-functioning pituitary adenomas (NFPAs), preoperative gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI radiomic features were associated with DNA methylation-defined risk strata (low-risk k1/k2 vs. high-risk k3–k5) previously linked to postoperative regrowth. The prespecified L1-penalized logistic regression model achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.69 and AUC of 0.73 (permutation p=0.001), with four radiomic features surviving Bonferroni correction. If validated externally, this approach could allow non-invasive preoperative risk stratification without requiring tumor tissue for methylation profiling. The authors are appropriately cautious: the model predicts a composite methylation label, not individual regrowth outcomes, and has not been independently validated.
items.caveat: Small single-center cohort (n=74); classifier predicts a methylation risk label, not directly validated against individual progression-free survival. Pooling k3–k5 as 'high risk' may obscure biologically distinct subgroups. External outcome-linked validation is explicitly required before clinical use.
items.quiz_question: A patient with a newly diagnosed non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma is undergoing preoperative planning. A colleague mentions that DNA methylation profiling can identify high-risk tumors prone to regrowth, but this requires surgical tissue. What does the THINKERS radiomics study suggest as a potential future alternative, and what are its current limitations?
items.quiz_answer: Preoperative MRI radiomic features derived from gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted sequences may non-invasively approximate methylation-defined risk strata associated with postoperative regrowth, potentially stratifying patients before surgery. However, the study is single-center, small (n=74), predicts a composite methylation label rather than individual regrowth probability, and requires external outcome-linked validation before it can influence clinical decision-making.

items.title: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 with concurrent Cushing's disease, prolactinoma, and multifocal pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors including insulinoma: a case report.
items.summary: This case documents a 28-year-old man with genetically confirmed MEN1 (splice-site variant c.825-1G>A) who simultaneously harbored ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism from a pituitary microadenoma, concurrent prolactinoma, primary hyperparathyroidism, and multifocal pancreatic NETs with biochemically confirmed insulinoma. Transsphenoidal surgery failed to achieve remission of Cushing's disease, and metyrapone provided only partial cortisol control, illustrating the refractory nature of MEN1-associated corticotroph tumors. Notably, lanreotide achieved complete resolution of hypoglycemia in the setting of multifocal insulinoma when a dominant lesion could not be localized even on 68Ga-NOTA-exendin-4 PET/CT, supporting a role for somatostatin analogs as a conservative bridge in this scenario. The case underscores how hormonal interactions between co-existing functioning tumors (e.g., hypercortisolism masking hypoglycemic symptoms) can significantly complicate recognition and management sequencing in MEN1.
items.caveat: Single case report; findings cannot be generalized. The favorable response to lanreotide for insulinoma in this context is anecdotal and should not replace standard surgical evaluation where feasible.
items.quiz_question: A 30-year-old man with known MEN1 presents with cushingoid features and episodic diaphoresis. Pituitary MRI shows a microadenoma; fasting glucose is 48 mg/dL. After transsphenoidal surgery fails to normalize cortisol, metyrapone is started. Subsequent workup confirms multifocal pancreatic NETs with biochemical insulinoma but no dominant lesion on functional imaging. What pharmacologic strategy is supported by this case for managing the insulinoma while awaiting further workup?
items.quiz_answer: Lanreotide (a somatostatin analog) achieved complete resolution of hypoglycemia in this MEN1 patient with multifocal insulinoma and no localizable dominant lesion, supporting its use as a conservative medical option when surgical targeting is not feasible.

items.title: [A rare case of Rosai-Dorfman disease involving the pituitary stalk and presenting initially with diabetes insipidus].
items.summary: This case describes a 38-year-old man with a 15-year course beginning with diabetes insipidus that ultimately progressed to panhypopituitarism, with MRI demonstrating marked pituitary stalk thickening and dural nodules. Pituitary stalk biopsy confirmed Rosai-Dorfman disease (RDD), a rare non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis, and molecular testing identified a BRAF V600E mutation. Treatment with the BRAF inhibitor dabrafenib produced meaningful structural response at 8 months — pituitary stalk thickening improved and both dural nodules resolved completely — alongside improved quality of life on hormone replacement. This case adds to the differential for pituitary stalk thickening and highlights BRAF V600E testing and targeted therapy as actionable steps when RDD is confirmed in the sellar region.
items.caveat: Single case report with only 8 months of follow-up on dabrafenib; long-term durability and pituitary function recovery are unknown. BRAF V600E prevalence in RDD is variable, so mutation testing should be pursued but negative results do not exclude the diagnosis.
items.quiz_question: A 40-year-old man presents with a 12-year history of central diabetes insipidus, now with new fatigue and cold intolerance. MRI shows a thickened pituitary stalk (7 mm) and two dural-based nodules. Anterior pituitary hormonal testing confirms panhypopituitarism. Stalk biopsy shows emperipolesis within large histiocytes. Molecular testing reveals BRAF V600E. What targeted therapy demonstrated structural and symptomatic benefit in an analogous published case?
items.quiz_answer: Dabrafenib, a BRAF inhibitor, produced reduction in pituitary stalk thickening and complete disappearance of dural nodules after 8 months of treatment in a BRAF V600E-positive Rosai-Dorfman disease case, alongside improved quality of life with concurrent pituitary hormone replacement.
